C114.notes: SER NA-MX-001. User shorthand 1914 + photo — and this one earns the long card. 1914 Chihuahua copper struck for the Ejército Constitucionalista while Francisco Villa’s División del Norte held the north: the old Chihuahua mint’s leftover presses, quiet since 1895, suddenly among the best-struck coinage of the whole Revolution. Engravers J. Salazar and M. Revilla cut the dies; Walrafen later mapped dozens of die marriages — common in absolute terms, endlessly variable up close. The copper itself is the story collectors retell from Fehrenbach: torn from telegraph and telephone wire across the vast Luis Terrazas estates after villistas seized the latifundio — wires that once carried a cattle baron’s messages, melted into pocket change for an army. Same calendar year Europe marched into WWI; in Chihuahua the Constitucionalista legend and a sword through a 5 bought tortillas and cartridges. First Mexico flip in this vault (silver Libertad is B007). Was once oldest flip (now Switzerland 1883 C242 / EU-CH-001). SER siblings: NA-MX-002…NA-MX-009. Mexico flips now 9.
C114.mint: revived Casa de Moneda de Chihuahua (closed 1895; machinery reused 1914–15)
C114.story: A 1914 5-centavo coin from Mexico. The front shows a liberty cap with rays and the words REPUBLICA MEXICANA and E. DE CHIHA. The back shows a large 5 pierced by an upright arrow, a centavo monogram, the words EJERCITO CONSTITUCIONALISTA and 1914, and often the name SALAZAR. Made of copper.
